en: I want to start with the tools and the
environment. As mentioned, as the user of an
agent, there is not too much you can do.
In tools like Claude Cowork, and it's the
same for all these general agents you can
install on your systems,
you don't necessarily see which tools an
agent has, and you also can't always edit
the tools.
Some agents do allow you to do that, but
many don't. But even in relatively
restrictive tools like Claude Cowork or
Claude Code, you can actually dive into the
settings, and often you have concepts like
plugins. In other tools, it might have a
different name, but the idea is that you can
install certain plugins that may be coming
from the official
company that built the agent, but also from
other developers and companies
that may equip an agent with new tools.
So there are ways of nudging the agent or
the agentic tool, the harness, into the
right direction. But again, it depends on
which tool you are using.
If you are building an agent, and that is
something we'll get back to later, you do of
course have not just the control, but also
the responsibility of making sure that you
equip your agent with the tools it needs.
That can be very specific tools if you're
building a task-specific agent,
and that could also be broader tools.
So that's the tools part. Now regarding the
environment, that includes things like the
sandbox. It simply means
where does your agent operate? What does it
see? If it's a general agent, which files
can it read, for example?
And here you have some influence both as the
user and the developer.
If you're the developer, you can control
what an agent can see by default. And for
example, the Claude Cowork team, like some
other agent developers as well,
made the decision that if you're starting a
new session in Claude Cowork, The agent by
default doesn't see anything on your system.
It can't read any files,
which probably makes sense. But there also
are agents which start with broader
permissions. It simply depends on which tool
you're using.
If you're the company building an agent,
that of course is an important decision. It
influences how your users can use that
agent. In Claude Cowork, for example,
you can assign a folder to an agent to give
it visibility into a certain
folder. And you could also select multiple
folders here if you wanted to, if you need
to work on multiple folders.
Once you do select such a folder here at the
example of Claude Cowork, but again, it's
similar in many other agents as well,
that folder is often placed in a so-called
sandbox, which means the agent can freely
work in that folder and indeed also edit or
write or delete files there. But it can't do
anything outside of that sandbox, outside of
that folder. It still can't touch other
places of your system. The agent runs in a
sandbox and only folders you added to the
sandbox are accessible.
That is one idea you'll find in many agents.
And again, if you're building an agent, you
have to decide whether you by default want
to restrict your agent and make sure that
your tools only work in a sandbox, Or if you
want to give those tools broader access and
allow them to edit anything on the system.
And that's therefore the tools and
environment part, which you have to consider
as the team building an agent, but also then
as the person or team using an agent, how
you use it and what you may need to do in
order to use it.
